prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the identification of its active peptide form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I confirm for the chair that my round-1 configuration names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, so the count is six of six for B016 as a single-part prize, with five of six on the Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio. My opening favoured Knudsen; I moved in round 1 and I have not moved again. The scientific case does not rest on that count. GLP-1 is an original discovery chain (proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, insulinotropic action in humans), repeatedly confirmed by independent groups over decades, and its consequences are now documented in large randomized trials for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. It is mature, and recognition is timely. The test I apply is the one a prize for discovery should apply: which contributions defined the biology, as distinct from which made the biology into a product. On that test the trio stands, with the therapeutic class named in the citation as the consequence of the discovery and not as the thing being honoured.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness and I cannot close it from the files I may read. Habener is outside the supplied credit list and is described as a possible priority claimant for the active peptide, and my own assessment of that priority record is from recollection, not from evidence in front of me. Any three names omit Knudsen, whose acylated analogue made the drugs practical, and the citation will be read as sidelining the people who made it a medicine. Mojsov's visibility in the literature is lower than that of Holst or Drucker, and a contested priority record weakens any trio. A single-part prize also leaves out other mature achievements, and if the committee judged the attribution burden of B016 to be unacceptable, the unfolded protein response (B010, Walter and Mori) remains the cleaner credit story, though with less direct clinical reach.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps Holst, Drucker and Knudsen with a citation that explicitly includes development of long-acting therapies, and regards the unfolded protein response as the scientifically cleanest discovery on the shortlist.
responses.response: I agree with Sandberg that Walter and Mori form the cleanest credit on the list, and I would not call B010 a weak candidate. We differ on the principle. If the citation includes long-acting therapy, Knudsen belongs; if it honours discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, Mojsov belongs. I prefer the second because the first turns a prize for discovery into one for a drug programme, and because the analogue was designed against a target already defined. Our past co-authorship does not touch this ballot. I do not see B010 as a second prize part: it would add a separate achievement to a prize whose first part is already contested, and it does not strengthen the GLP-1 case.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved from Knudsen to Mojsov on the grounds that identifying the biologically active peptide is a discovery step the analogues depended on, and asks that the scientific case be tested and not assumed.
responses.response: I take her request seriously, and the answer is that the case holds when tested without reference to the count: the discovery chain is original, independently confirmed, and the clinical outcome data are strong. Her reasoning for Mojsov matches mine, and we reached it from the same starting point on the third name. Where I would add a caution is the weight she places on the active-peptide step: it is real, but its priority is contested and involves Habener, so the citation should name the identification of the active form without asserting sole priority. I also agree with her view that a second part such as TOR or CAR-T would add attribution problems that GLP-1 alone avoids.

responses.point: The chair, in the round-1 summary, asks whether the third name should be Mojsov or Knudsen, whether B016 should stand alone, and notes that long-term safety of chronic incretin therapy is still accumulating.
responses.response: My answers to the chair are these. Third name: Mojsov, on the discovery-first reading, as a close call. Alone or with a second part: alone. Citation: it should mention therapy only as the consequence of the discovery, and I have worded it accordingly. On long-term safety, I agree it is still accumulating, but it concerns the drugs and not the discovery, and it does not change the scientific assessment of the physiology. A prize in this area could be read as a commercial endorsement, which is one more reason to keep the citation tied to the physiology and not to a product.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treating Knudsen's role as industrial, and keeps the unfolded protein response as a first alternative with a more compact credit story.
responses.response: I agree with the trio. I would resist describing Knudsen's contribution as merely industrial, since the design of a long-acting analogue was real science, and my preference rests on a narrower point: it is development against a defined target, not discovery of the hormone or its active form. Perlmann says Mojsov's role is less visible in the literature, and I accept that. Visibility is not the criterion, but it does mean the committee must be sure of the priority record, and I would want that verified before the final ballot is treated as settled.

uncertainties: Priority for identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, including the contribution of Habener, cannot be verified from the files I may read, and a trio that rests on it carries that uncertainty.
Whether drug-development contributions such as Knudsen's should rank with discovery in a prize for discovery; I have settled on discovery first, as a close call.
Whether a second distinct part would strengthen the configuration; I judge that it would mainly add attribution burden.
Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating, though this concerns the drugs more than the discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My documented connections are co-authorship of the 2016 spatial-transcriptomics paper and earlier papers with Rickard Sandberg, which are unrelated to the shortlisted discoveries, and I infer no personal ties from shared institutions. No recusal is requested and my disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
